description: We are exploring “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling About NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.” Our goal is to uncover the stories behind spacecraft, rovers, landers, and equipment left behind during space exploration. We aim to combine space science, research, and creative storytelling to bring these forgotten objects back into the spotlight. We welcome teammates interested in astronomy, research, writing, creativity, and communication!
summary:
Echoes Beyond Earth by Team AXEELL is a mobile-first, interactive web field journal built for the "Abandoned, but Not Forgotten" challenge. Developed using open web technologies (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) and powered by verified NASA open data, the platform transforms discarded space hardware into accessible human stories.
Rather than treating retired equipment as mere space debris, our application guides users through a five-step interactive journey across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Users can explore a curated Field Archive featuring five iconic artifacts—including Apollo lunar rovers and laser retroreflectors, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, and Voyager 1—trace their missions through an interactive chronological timeline, test their knowledge with a clue-based quiz, and verify every fact against linked NASA archival records.
By turning complex archival datasets into a cohesive, accessible digital experience that runs on any device without installation, Echoes Beyond Earth preserves humanity’s off-world heritage and makes space exploration inspiring and easy for anyone to follow.
details:
AXEELL: Echoes Beyond Earth is a mobile-first interactive field journal about hardware NASA left on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. Visitors follow a photo-story trail, explore an artifact archive (Lunar Roving Vehicle, Apollo laser retroreflector, Sojourner, Pathfinder and its airbags, Voyager 1), travel a 1969–1997 timeline, and take a short quiz that reveals field-note clues. Every field note links to its NASA source record.

Benefits and intended impact: it makes space heritage easy to understand for students and the public. It shows that “abandoned” equipment still carries science (the Apollo reflectors are still used for lunar laser ranging) and human stories. It also builds the habit of checking sources.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single mobile-first web page, using Google Fonts (Space Grotesk, DM Sans, DM Mono). Our submission slides were made with PptxGenJS and the demo video with Python (Pillow) and FFmpeg.

Creativity: we treat each object as “a message in place” and tell the story as a field journal, not a data dashboard. It combines archival photos, short original notes and a quiz.

Factors considered: accuracy (facts only from NASA records), readability on phones, no install needed, short text, and credit for every image.
